problem: File cannot be read as an RSMF file
what_it_means: The program could not read this file at all. It is probably damaged, incomplete, or not really an RSMF file.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads the file the way an email program reads an .eml file: a block of labelled lines at the top, followed by one or more parts. If that structure cannot be read, this rule fires.
why_it_matters: An RSMF file is an email file with a different ending. If it cannot be read as one, neither this app nor Relativity can reach the messages inside it.
what_to_do: Copy the file again from where it came from and scan it again. If it still fails, ask whoever produced the file for a new copy.
technical_check: File parses as an Internet Message Format / MIME message
technical_detail: The file could not be read as an email-style (MIME) message at all. An RSMF file is an .eml file with a different extension, so this usually means the file is truncated, corrupted, or is not an RSMF file. Check that the file transferred completely (compare its size with the source). If it did, the file is not a valid RSMF. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.

problem: Version label is missing
what_it_means: Every RSMF file is meant to start with a label saying which version of the format it uses. This file has none, and Relativity requires it.
how_it_is_checked: The app looks through the labelled lines at the top of the file for one named X-RSMF-Version and checks that it has a value.
why_it_matters: Relativity's specification makes this the one required label. It says which version of the format the rest of the file follows.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the files to make them again with the version label included.
technical_check: X-RSMF-Version header present
technical_detail: The X-RSMF-Version header is missing or empty. Relativity requires it in both RSMF 1.0 and 2.0. Add an X-RSMF-Version header (for example 2.0.0) as the first header line, matching the version in rsmf_manifest.json. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.

problem: Version label is not one Relativity documents
what_it_means: The file's version label says something other than 1.0.0 or 2.0.0, the only two versions Relativity documents.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads the value of the X-RSMF-Version label and compares it with the two documented versions, 1.0.0 and 2.0.0.
why_it_matters: Relativity has published the format for those two versions only. With any other value it is not clear which set of rules the file is meant to follow.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the files to make them again as version 1.0.0 or 2.0.0.
technical_check: X-RSMF-Version value is a supported version
technical_detail: The X-RSMF-Version header holds a value other than 1.0.0 or 2.0.0, the two versions Relativity has published schemas for. Set X-RSMF-Version to 1.0.0 or 2.0.0 to match the manifest. Whether Relativity accepts shortened forms such as 2.0 is not documented, so use the full form.

problem: Version label is not on the first line
what_it_means: The file has its version label, but another line comes before it, usually the name of the tool that made the file. Relativity's instructions say the version label should come first. They say "should", not "must", and this program cannot tell you whether Relativity will mind.
how_it_is_checked: The app checks which labelled line comes first in the file and whether that line is X-RSMF-Version.
why_it_matters: Relativity's instructions for creating a file say the version label should be the first line. They do not say what happens when it is not, which is why this is a warning and not an error.
what_to_do: There is nothing to fix by hand inside each file. Load a small test batch into Relativity to confirm the files are accepted, and tell whoever runs the export tool so they can change the order if needed.
technical_check: X-RSMF-Version is the first header line
technical_detail: X-RSMF-Version is present but is not the first header line. Relativity's documentation says it should be first. Move X-RSMF-Version to the top of the headers. The documentation says "should", so treat this as a warning to correct at the source, not proof the file will be rejected.

problem: The file does not hold exactly one message package
what_it_means: An RSMF file must carry one package inside it, named rsmf.zip, which holds the messages. This file has none, more than one, or one with the wrong name.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the attached parts of the file and checks that there is exactly one, that it is named rsmf.zip, that it is marked as an attachment and that it is base64-encoded.
why_it_matters: Relativity expects all of a file's messages and attachments inside that single package. Relativity's own validator fails a file that carries a second attachment.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again. This cannot be repaired by hand.
technical_check: Exactly one base64 attachment with filename rsmf.zip
technical_detail: The file does not have exactly one attachment named rsmf.zip, base64-encoded and marked as an attachment. There may be none, more than one, a different name or letter case, or a different encoding. The file must contain a single attachment: Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="rsmf.zip", Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64. Remove any other attachments; put every message attachment inside rsmf.zip instead.

problem: The message package inside the file is damaged
what_it_means: The package of messages inside this file cannot be opened, usually because the file was cut short or damaged while being copied.
how_it_is_checked: The app decodes the rsmf.zip attachment from base64 text back into a ZIP archive and then tries to open the archive.
why_it_matters: Everything a reviewer would see is inside that archive. If it cannot be opened, there are no messages to load or view.
what_to_do: Copy the file again from where it came from and scan it again. If it still fails, ask whoever produced the file for a new copy.
technical_check: rsmf.zip decodes from base64 and opens as a ZIP archive
technical_detail: The rsmf.zip attachment could not be decoded or opened: it contains characters that are not base64, or the decoded data is not a readable ZIP archive (often because it was cut short). Check that the file transferred completely. If it did, the archive was damaged when the file was built. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.

problem: File name does not end in .rsmf
what_it_means: Relativity recognises these files by the .rsmf ending on the file name, and this file has a different ending.
how_it_is_checked: The app looks at the ending of the file's name.
why_it_matters: Relativity's documentation lists the .rsmf ending first among the things Processing needs in order to treat a file as RSMF.
what_to_do: Rename the file so that its name ends in .rsmf.
technical_check: File name extension
technical_detail: The file name does not end in .rsmf. Relativity Processing identifies RSMF files by this extension. Rename the file so it ends in .rsmf.

problem: A custom label has a name that is too long
what_it_means: The file carries an extra, custom label whose name is 255 characters or longer. Relativity says such names must be shorter.
how_it_is_checked: The app measures the name of every extra X-RSMF label that is not one of the standard ones.
why_it_matters: Relativity documents that the name of a custom label must be shorter than 255 characters.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to shorten that label's name.
technical_check: Custom X-RSMF-* header name length
technical_detail: A custom X-RSMF-* header has a name of 255 characters or more. Relativity documents that a custom header name must be shorter than 255 characters. Shorten the custom header's name at the source.
documentation: Relativity help: Processing an RSMF file (see: RSMF Header) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Processing_an_RSMF_file.htm

problem: A summary value at the top of the file is the wrong kind
what_it_means: The top of the file can carry summary values such as counts and dates. One of them holds something that is not a number, or not a date. Relativity copies these values into its own fields, so that field would be wrong or empty.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads the optional count and date labels at the top of the file and tries to read each one as a whole number or as a standard date and time.
why_it_matters: Relativity copies these values into document fields. A value of the wrong kind leaves that field wrong or empty.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to correct the value or leave it out; these summary values are optional.
technical_check: Optional count and date headers are parseable
technical_detail: An optional roll-up header holds a value of the wrong kind: X-RSMF-EventCount or X-RSMF-AttachmentCount is not a whole number, or X-RSMF-BeginDate or X-RSMF-EndDate is not an ISO 8601 date-time. Correct the header value, or remove the header: these headers are optional. Relativity maps them to fields, so a bad value gives a wrong or empty field.

problem: Stated number of events does not match the content
what_it_means: The summary at the top of the file says it holds a certain number of events, but the content holds a different number. Relativity can copy the stated number into a field, so that field would be wrong.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the events in the list of messages and compares the total with the number stated in the X-RSMF-EventCount label.
why_it_matters: Relativity can copy the stated count into a field, and a mismatch can also be a sign that events were lost when the file was made.
what_to_do: Compare the Observed column with what you expect from the source, in case events are missing. Then ask whoever produced the file to correct the count.
technical_check: X-RSMF-EventCount matches the number of events in the manifest
technical_detail: X-RSMF-EventCount does not equal the number of events in the manifest. The header is mapped to a field in Relativity, so the field would be wrong. Set X-RSMF-EventCount to the number of events in rsmf_manifest.json. This tool compares it with all events (not only messages); the published sources are not explicit on that point.

problem: Stated start date does not match the first message
what_it_means: The summary at the top of the file gives a start date and time, but the earliest message in the file is at a different time. Relativity can use the stated start date as the document's sent date, so sorting and filtering by date could be off for this file.
how_it_is_checked: The app finds the earliest event time in the file and compares it, as a moment in time, with the X-RSMF-BeginDate label.
why_it_matters: Relativity can use the stated start date as the document's sent date, so a wrong value affects sorting and filtering by date.
what_to_do: Look at the Observed column to see how far apart the two times are. A small gap is often rounding or a time-zone slip in the export tool. A large gap deserves a question to whoever produced the file. Correcting it means making the file again.
technical_check: X-RSMF-BeginDate matches the earliest event timestamp
technical_detail: X-RSMF-BeginDate is not the same moment as the earliest event timestamp in the manifest. Relativity can map this header to the sent date. Set X-RSMF-BeginDate to the earliest event timestamp. Differences of time zone notation are fine; the two must be the same instant.

problem: Stated end date does not match the last message
what_it_means: The summary at the top of the file gives an end date and time, but the latest message in the file is at a different time. Relativity can use the stated end date as the document's last-modified date, so sorting and filtering by date could be off for this file.
how_it_is_checked: The app finds the latest event time in the file and compares it, as a moment in time, with the X-RSMF-EndDate label.
why_it_matters: Relativity can use the stated end date as the document's last-modified date, so a wrong value affects sorting and filtering by date.
what_to_do: Look at the Observed column to see how far apart the two times are. A small gap is often rounding or a time-zone slip in the export tool. A large gap deserves a question to whoever produced the file. Correcting it means making the file again.
technical_check: X-RSMF-EndDate matches the latest event timestamp
technical_detail: X-RSMF-EndDate is not the same moment as the latest event timestamp in the manifest. Relativity can map this header to the last-modified date. Set X-RSMF-EndDate to the latest event timestamp. Differences of time zone notation are fine; the two must be the same instant.

problem: File says version 1.0 but uses a version 2.0 feature
what_it_means: The file is labelled as version 1.0, but the top of the file includes a summary value that only exists in version 2.0.
how_it_is_checked: When the file says it is version 1.0.0, the app looks for the labels that exist only in version 2.0.
why_it_matters: The specification's table of labels marks these as version 2.0 only, so the file is mixing two versions of the format.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again as version 2.0, or to leave that value out.
technical_check: RSMF 2.0-only header in a 1.0.0 file
technical_detail: The file declares RSMF 1.0.0 but carries a header that only exists in RSMF 2.0 (Application, Custodian, Participants, AttachmentCount or EventCollectionID). Either produce the file as RSMF 2.0.0 (header and manifest), or remove the 2.0-only header.

problem: The list of messages is missing from the file
what_it_means: Inside every RSMF file there is one list that holds all the messages. In this file it is missing, misnamed, or tucked inside a subfolder, so there is nothing to review.
how_it_is_checked: The app lists the contents of rsmf.zip and looks for a file named exactly rsmf_manifest.json at the top level, not inside a folder.
why_it_matters: The specification puts the list of messages in that one file at the top level of the archive. Without it there is nothing to show.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again. This cannot be repaired by hand.
technical_check: rsmf_manifest.json exists at the ZIP root
technical_detail: rsmf.zip opened, but there is no rsmf_manifest.json at its top level. The manifest holds every message, so without it there is nothing to review. It may be missing, inside a subfolder, or named with different letter case. Rebuild rsmf.zip so that rsmf_manifest.json sits at the root of the archive, not inside a folder.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: RSMF structure) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: The file contains an item that no message refers to
what_it_means: The package inside this file holds an extra item, such as a picture or document, that no message, profile picture or icon points to. Relativity would load it as a separate loose document, not as part of a message.
how_it_is_checked: The app lists every item in rsmf.zip and checks whether any attachment, profile picture or conversation icon refers to it by name.
why_it_matters: An item that nothing refers to is not shown as part of any message. Relativity's processing documentation covers such items under troubleshooting attachments.
what_to_do: Decide whether the item belongs to a message. If it does, ask whoever produced the file to link it to that message. If it does not, ask them to leave it out.
technical_check: ZIP member is not referenced by the manifest
technical_detail: rsmf.zip contains a file that no attachment, avatar or icon in the manifest refers to. Relativity processes such a file as a loose document under an rsmf.zip folder, not as part of a message. If the file belongs to a message, add an attachment entry for it to that event (the id must equal the file name). If it does not belong, remove it from the archive.
documentation: Relativity help: Processing an RSMF file (see: RSMF.zip, Troubleshooting attachments) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Processing_an_RSMF_file.htm

problem: The list of messages cannot be read
what_it_means: The list of messages inside this file is damaged or not written correctly, so no messages could be read from it.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads rsmf_manifest.json as JSON, the structured text format it must be written in, and checks that the whole file is a single object.
why_it_matters: Every message is stored in this one file. If it is not valid JSON, none of the messages can be read.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again. The Observed column says where the list breaks, which will help them.
technical_check: Manifest is well-formed JSON with an object root
technical_detail: rsmf_manifest.json is not valid JSON (or its top level is not an object), so no message could be read from it. Open the manifest from the Raw manifest tab to see where it breaks; the finding gives the line and position. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: rsmf_manifest.json) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: The list of messages does not state a valid version
what_it_means: The list of messages inside the file should say it is version 1.0.0 or 2.0.0. It says something else, or nothing, so the detailed format checks could not be run.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads the version value inside the list of messages and compares it with 1.0.0 and 2.0.0.
why_it_matters: The version decides which of Relativity's two published format definitions the content is checked against.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again with the version stated.
technical_check: Manifest version is a supported version
technical_detail: The manifest's "version" is missing or is not 1.0.0 or 2.0.0, so the tool cannot tell which schema applies and schema validation was skipped. Set "version" in rsmf_manifest.json to 1.0.0 or 2.0.0, matching the X-RSMF-Version header.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: rsmf_manifest.json) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm; Relativity on GitHub: RSMF validator samples and schema (see: schemas) https://github.com/relativitydev/rsmf-validator-samples

problem: Content breaks Relativity's published format rules
what_it_means: Something Relativity's format requires is missing, or is written in the wrong way. The Observed and Location columns say what and where. Relativity's own checker treats these as errors.
how_it_is_checked: The app checks the list of messages against the format definition (the schema) that Relativity publishes for the file's version. Each thing the definition does not allow is reported separately, with its location.
why_it_matters: The schema is Relativity's own statement of which fields are required and how they must be written. Relativity's validator reports these problems as failures.
what_to_do: Send the finding to whoever produced the file and ask them to correct it and make the file again.
technical_check: Manifest validates against the bundled schema for its version
technical_detail: The manifest breaks Relativity's published schema for its version: a required field is missing, a value has the wrong type, or a value is not one of the allowed choices. The message and location say exactly what and where. Correct the field named in the location. Relativity's own validator reports schema violations as errors. Note that RSMF 1.0 requires more fields than 2.0 (for example display names, event participant, conversation and timestamp).
documentation: Relativity on GitHub: RSMF validator samples and schema (see: rsmf_schema_1_0_0.json / rsmf_schema_2_0_0.json, the walkthrough PDF) https://github.com/relativitydev/rsmf-validator-samples

problem: Content includes a field Relativity's format does not define
what_it_means: The file contains a piece of information under a name the format does not know. It is often a misspelt name, or a version 2.0 feature used in a version 1.0 file. Relativity's checker warns about this, and the information may be ignored.
how_it_is_checked: The app compares every field name in the list of messages with the names the schema defines for that version of the format.
why_it_matters: A name the format does not define is usually a misspelling or a field from the other version. Relativity's validator warns about it, and the information may be ignored.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to use the documented name, or to move the information into the format's place for custom values.
technical_check: Property is not defined by the schema for this version
technical_detail: The manifest contains a property the schema for its version does not define. It is often a misspelling (for example "attachment" for "attachments") or an RSMF 2.0 field used in a 1.0 file. Relativity's validator reports this as a warning. Rename the property to the documented name, or move the value into the record's "custom" list, which is the supported place for extra metadata.

problem: No participants are listed
what_it_means: The file does not list anyone as taking part in the conversation. Relativity requires at least one participant.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the entries in the participants list.
why_it_matters: The specification requires at least one participant, because every message has to belong to someone.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again with the participants included.
technical_check: At least one participant
technical_detail: The manifest has no participants. Relativity requires at least one for a file to be valid. Add every person or account that takes part to the "participants" list. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: Participants) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: No conversations are listed
what_it_means: The file does not contain any conversation. Relativity requires at least one.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the entries in the conversations list.
why_it_matters: The specification requires at least one conversation, because every message has to belong to one.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make it again.
technical_check: At least one conversation
technical_detail: The manifest has no conversations. Relativity requires at least one for a file to be valid. Add the conversation the events belong to. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: Conversations) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: The file contains no messages or events
what_it_means: The file is well formed but empty: it holds no messages at all.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the entries in the events list, which holds the messages and other activity.
why_it_matters: A file with no events has nothing to review, which usually means the export covered the wrong dates or went wrong.
what_to_do: Check that the export covered the dates you intended. If it did, this file may simply be empty and not needed.
technical_check: At least one event
technical_detail: The manifest has no events, so the file contains no messages. Check the export covered the intended date range. Regenerate the file with the tool that created it, or ask the party who supplied it for a corrected file.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: Events) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: Two participants share the same ID
what_it_means: Each participant should have an ID of their own. Two or more share one here, so messages could be shown under the wrong person.
how_it_is_checked: The app collects every participant ID in the file and looks for any value that is used more than once.
why_it_matters: Messages name their sender by ID. If two people share an ID, a message could be shown under the wrong person.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to give each participant a separate ID and make the file again.
technical_check: Participant ids are unique
technical_detail: Two or more participants share the same id. Events refer to participants by id, so messages could be attributed to the wrong person. Give every participant a unique id and update the references that use it.
documentation: Relativity help: The Relativity Short Message Format (RSMF) (see: Participants (id)) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/System_Guides/Relativity_Short_Message_Format/Relativity_short_message_format.htm

problem: Two conversations share the same ID
what_it_means: Each conversation should have an ID of its own. Two or more share one here, so messages cannot be tied to the right conversation.
how_it_is_checked: The app collects every conversation ID in the file and looks for any value that is used more than once.
why_it_matters: Messages name their conversation by ID. If two conversations share an ID, messages cannot be tied to the right one.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to give each conversation a separate ID and make the file again.
technical_check: Conversation ids are unique
technical_detail: Two or more conversations share the same id, so events cannot be tied to one conversation unambiguously. Give every conversation a unique id and update the events that refer to it.

problem: Two messages in one conversation share the same ID
what_it_means: Replies point to the message they answer by its ID. Two or more messages share an ID here, so a reply could attach to the wrong message.
how_it_is_checked: Within each conversation, the app collects the event IDs that are present and looks for any value that is used more than once.
why_it_matters: Replies point to the message they answer by its ID. If two messages share an ID, a reply could attach to the wrong one.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to give each message a separate ID and make the file again.
technical_check: Event ids are unique within their conversation
technical_detail: Two or more events in the same conversation share an id. Replies refer to their parent by id, so threads could attach to the wrong message. Give each event in a conversation a unique id (ids are only needed for events that are part of a thread).

problem: A conversation does not say whether it is a direct chat or a channel
what_it_means: Version 2.0 files are meant to say, for each conversation, whether it is a direct chat between fixed people or a channel people can join and leave. This one does not say.
how_it_is_checked: For version 2.0.0 files, the app checks that each conversation states a type.
why_it_matters: The specification lists the type (direct or channel) as required in version 2.0, although the published schema does not enforce it.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to add that information.
technical_check: Conversation type present in a 2.0.0 manifest
technical_detail: A conversation in an RSMF 2.0 file has no "type". Relativity's specification page lists it as required (direct or channel) although the 2.0 schema does not enforce it. Add "type": "direct" (fixed set of participants) or "channel" (participants can join and leave).

problem: A reaction's name is too long
what_it_means: A reaction, such as a thumbs-up, is recorded with a name longer than the 30 characters Relativity allows.
how_it_is_checked: The app measures the length of each reaction's value.
why_it_matters: The specification limits a reaction's value to 30 characters. The published schema states this limit in a way that has no effect, so the app checks it directly.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to use a short name or the emoji itself.
technical_check: Reaction value length
technical_detail: A reaction's value is longer than 30 characters, the documented maximum. Use a short code or the emoji character itself for the reaction value.

problem: A date and time is not written in the standard way
what_it_means: A date and time in the file cannot be read as a date. If it is the time of a message, this program also cannot judge the one-day and 24-hour checks for the file.
how_it_is_checked: The app tries to read the time on every event, edit and read receipt as a standard ISO 8601 date and time.
why_it_matters: Messages are put in order and displayed by these times, and this app's one-day and 24-hour checks depend on them too.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to write dates in the standard international form, including the time zone.
technical_check: Timestamp is an ISO 8601 date-time
technical_detail: A timestamp on an event, edit or read receipt is not an ISO 8601 date-time (for example 2026-03-03T14:05:00Z). Write the timestamp in ISO 8601 form with a time zone offset or Z. If it is a message's own timestamp, the time-window check for the file will also be indeterminate until it is fixed.

problem: A conversation lists someone who is not in the participant list
what_it_means: A conversation names a participant that the file's list of participants does not include. Relativity's checker warns about this.
how_it_is_checked: The app takes each participant ID listed on a conversation and looks it up in the file's participant list.

what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to add the missing person to the participant list.
technical_check: Conversation participant maps to a root participant
technical_detail: A conversation lists a participant id that is not defined in the manifest's participants. Relativity's validator reports this as a warning. Add the missing participant to the participants list, or correct the id in the conversation.

technical_detail: An event's participant (the sender) is not defined in the manifest's participants, so the message has no known sender. Relativity's validator reports this as a warning. Add the missing participant, or correct the id on the event.

what_it_means: A message points to a conversation that is not in the file, so it does not belong anywhere.

what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to correct the message or add the missing conversation.
technical_check: Event conversation maps to a conversation
technical_detail: An event refers to a conversation id that does not exist, so it belongs to no conversation. Correct the event's "conversation" to an existing conversation id, or add the missing conversation.

problem: A reply answers a message that is not in this file
what_it_means: A reply points to an earlier message that this file does not contain. That is normal when one long conversation has been split into several files and the earlier message is in another file.
how_it_is_checked: The app takes the parent ID on each reply and looks for an event with that ID in the same file.
why_it_matters: Replies are shown linked to the message they answer. Relativity's slicing documentation notes that splitting a conversation into files can separate a reply from its parent.
what_to_do: If your files are slices of longer conversations, this usually needs no action. Otherwise ask whoever produced the file to check it.
technical_check: Event parent maps to another event in the same conversation
technical_detail: A reply's "parent" is not the id of another event in the same conversation. This also happens legitimately when a long conversation is split into several files and the original message is in a different file. If the parent should be in this file, correct the id. If the file is one slice of a longer conversation, this may be expected: note it and move on.

technical_detail: A conversation's custodian is not one of that conversation's participants. The custodian is the person the data was collected from. Set "custodian" to the id of a participant in the conversation, or add that participant to the conversation.

problem: A message's attachment is missing from the file
what_it_means: A message says it has an attachment, but that attachment is not inside the RSMF file, so reviewers will not be able to open it.
how_it_is_checked: The app takes the ID of each attachment listed on an event and looks for an item with that name inside rsmf.zip.
why_it_matters: The message says it has an attachment, but the attachment's content is not in the file, so it cannot be reviewed.
what_to_do: Check whether the attachment exists in the source data. If it does, ask whoever produced the file to make it again with the attachment included.
technical_check: Attachment id resolves to a file in rsmf.zip
technical_detail: An event lists an attachment whose id is not the name of any file in rsmf.zip, so the attachment cannot be shown or linked to the message. Relativity's validator reports the same condition. Add the file to rsmf.zip under exactly that name (including extension), or correct the attachment id. Names are compared exactly, including letter case.

problem: File is larger than the size limit
what_it_means: The file is bigger than the size limit set in Settings. Relativity says RSMF files over 2 GB are not supported and may fail to process.
how_it_is_checked: The app reads the file's size in bytes and compares it with the size limit in Settings, which is 2 GB unless you change it.
why_it_matters: Relativity's documentation states that RSMF files greater than 2 GB are not supported.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to split the conversation into smaller files, for example by shorter time periods.
technical_check: File size is within the processing size threshold
technical_detail: The file is larger than the size threshold. Relativity documents that RSMF files greater than 2 GB are not supported and may be unable to process. Split the conversation into smaller files (for example smaller time periods) with the tool that generated it. The threshold used is stated in the reports; the default is 2,147,483,648 bytes.

what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to split the conversation into files of 10,000 or fewer, usually by shorter time periods.
technical_check: Total events are within the viewer limit
technical_detail: The file has more than 10,000 events. Relativity documents a viewer limit of 10,000 events per RSMF file and says larger files may cause errors when opened. Split the conversation into files of 10,000 events or fewer, typically by a shorter time period.

problem: Messages fall on more than one calendar day
what_it_means: This is your own team's check, not a Relativity requirement. The messages in this file fall on more than one calendar day in the time zone chosen in Settings.
how_it_is_checked: The app converts every message time into the time zone chosen in Settings and checks whether they all fall on the same calendar date.
why_it_matters: This is a local QC rule for teams that expect one file per day. It is not a Relativity requirement, and it can be switched off with the time-window mode in Settings.
what_to_do: First check the time zone in Settings, because the same file can pass in one zone and fail in another. If the zone is right and you need one day per file, ask for the files to be split by day.
technical_check: All message timestamps fall on one calendar day in the selected time zone
technical_detail: Local QC rule A: the messages in this file fall on more than one calendar day in the selected time zone. Each timestamp is converted from its own offset first. If one-day files are required, regenerate with daily slicing in the intended time zone. Check the time zone setting first: the same file can pass in one zone and fail in another.
source: BRIEF Phase 1 Time-window QC, Rule A
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: Messages span more than 24 hours
what_it_means: This is your own team's check, not a Relativity requirement. The last message in this file is more than 24 hours after the first.
how_it_is_checked: The app subtracts the earliest message time in the file from the latest and checks whether the difference is more than 24 hours.
why_it_matters: This is a local QC rule for teams that expect each file to cover no more than a day. It is not a Relativity requirement.
what_to_do: If you need each file to cover 24 hours or less, ask for the files to be split into shorter periods.
technical_check: Elapsed span between earliest and latest message
technical_detail: Local QC rule B: the latest message is more than 24 hours after the earliest. Exactly 24 hours passes. Regenerate with a shorter time period per file. On the day clocks go back, one calendar day lasts 25 hours, so a file can pass rule A and still fail this rule.
source: BRIEF Phase 1 Time-window QC, Rule B
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: Message times do not say which time zone they are in
what_it_means: Some message times in this file do not say which time zone they are in. This program treated them as UTC, which may be several hours away from what was meant, so the one-day check could be wrong.
how_it_is_checked: The app checks whether each message time states its offset from UTC, for example Z or -05:00.
why_it_matters: A time without an offset is ambiguous. The app treats it as UTC, which can move a message onto a different calendar day.
what_to_do: Treat the one-day and 24-hour results for this file with caution, and ask whoever produced the file to include the time zone with each time.
technical_check: Message timestamp has no UTC offset; treated as UTC
technical_detail: One or more message timestamps have no time zone offset. The tool reads them as UTC, which may not be what the source system meant, so day boundaries could be wrong. Have the generating tool write timestamps with an offset or Z. Until then, treat the time-window result for this file with caution.
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: More participants than the limit you set
what_it_means: The file has more participants than the warning number you entered in Settings. Relativity says files with very many participants can be slow, but gives no number.
how_it_is_checked: The app counts the distinct participants in the file and compares the total with the warning threshold in Settings. The check is off while that box is blank.
why_it_matters: This is a local QC rule for spotting unusually large conversations. It is not a Relativity requirement.
what_to_do: Decide whether the conversation should be split, or raise your warning number. This is your own check, not a Relativity limit.
technical_check: Unique participant count is within the user-set threshold
technical_detail: The file has more unique participants than the warning threshold you set. Relativity says files with a significant number of participants cause performance problems but publishes no number. Decide whether the conversation should be split or the threshold raised. This is a local warning, not a Relativity limit.
documentation: Relativity help: Workflow solutions for very large workspaces (see: RSMF) https://help.relativity.com/RelativityOne/Content/Solutions/Workflow_solutions_for_very_large_workspaces.htm

problem: A participant is called "Unspecified Sender"
what_it_means: "Unspecified Sender" is a placeholder that an export tool writes when it could not tell who sent a message. Messages from this participant are not tied to a real person.
how_it_is_checked: The app looks at each participant's display name, account ID and ID for the words Unspecified Sender, in any letter case.
why_it_matters: That placeholder means the export tool could not tell who sent the messages, so reviewers will not be able to tell either.
what_to_do: Ask whoever ran the export whether the real sender can be identified; often it is the owner of the device. If not, make a note that these messages have no named sender.
technical_check: No participant is the placeholder "Unspecified Sender"
technical_detail: A participant is named "Unspecified Sender". That is a placeholder some export tools write when they could not work out who sent a message, so messages from this participant are not attributed to a real person. Go back to the source data or the export settings and get the real sender identified, then regenerate the file. If the sender truly cannot be known, record that decision.
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: A participant shows only as a phone number
what_it_means: No name is recorded for this person, so reviewers will see a phone number where a name would normally be. The file is not damaged.
how_it_is_checked: The app looks for participants with no email address whose display name and account ID are each blank or a phone number.
why_it_matters: Reviewers see a number where a name should be, which makes it hard to tell who was speaking.
what_to_do: If names matter for the review, ask whoever ran the export whether contact names can be included, for example from the phone's address book, and the files made again. If the numbers cannot be matched to names, this is simply how the data is.
technical_check: Every participant has a name, not only a phone number
technical_detail: A participant is identified by a phone number alone: there is no display name, account name or email address. Reviewers will see only the number. If the name behind the number is known (for example from the device's contacts), add it as the participant's display name and regenerate the file. Otherwise record that the number could not be resolved.
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: The file gives two different version numbers
what_it_means: The version label at the top of the file and the version stated inside it disagree, so it is unclear which version of the format the file follows.
how_it_is_checked: The app compares the version stated in the X-RSMF-Version label with the version stated inside the list of messages.
why_it_matters: If the two disagree, it is unclear which version of the format the file follows, and so which rules apply to it.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to make the two agree.
technical_check: X-RSMF-Version header equals manifest version
technical_detail: The X-RSMF-Version header and the manifest's "version" disagree, so it is unclear which version of the format the file follows. Make the header and the manifest state the same version.
documentation: Relativity on GitHub: RSMF generation sample (see: RSMFGenerator.cs) https://github.com/relativitydev/relativity-rsmf-gen-sample

problem: The file could not be opened
what_it_means: The program could not open or read this file. It may be open in another program, you may not have permission, or the disk reported a problem. Nothing in the file was checked, so this is not a pass.
how_it_is_checked: The app tries to open and read the file. If Windows refuses, this rule records the reason.
why_it_matters: A file that could not be read was not checked, so it must not be mistaken for a clean file.
what_to_do: Close any program that has the file open, check that you can open the folder, and scan again.
technical_check: File could not be opened or read
technical_detail: The file could not be opened or read (it may be locked by another program, you may lack permission, or the disk reported an error). Nothing in it was checked, so this is not a pass. Close any program that has the file open, check your access to it, and scan again.
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: A folder could not be opened
what_it_means: The program could not look inside one folder, usually because of permissions. Any RSMF files in it were not seen, so the scan is incomplete.
how_it_is_checked: The app tries to list the contents of every folder under the one you chose. If Windows refuses, this rule records the folder.
why_it_matters: Any files in that folder were never seen, so the scan does not cover everything you pointed it at.
what_to_do: Get access to the folder, or scan a copy of it, and run the scan again.
technical_check: Directory could not be listed; scan coverage incomplete
technical_detail: A folder could not be listed, usually because of permissions. Any RSMF files inside it were not seen, so the scan is incomplete. Get access to the folder, or scan a copy of it, and run the scan again.
documentation: No Relativity page: this is the app's own check.

problem: Part of the file was too large to check
what_it_means: Part of this file was larger than the program's safety limit, so some checks were not run. This is not a pass.
how_it_is_checked: The app measures each item inside the archive before loading it and skips any that is larger than its memory safety limit.
why_it_matters: Content that was skipped was not checked, and the report says so instead of passing the file silently.
what_to_do: A file this large usually means the conversation should be split into smaller files. Ask whoever produced it.
technical_check: Content exceeded the in-memory size cap; dependent checks not run
technical_detail: Part of the file was larger than the tool's in-memory safety cap, so the checks that need it were not run. This is not a pass. For rsmf.zip, scan through the app or CLI with an output folder so the archive can be spooled to disk. A manifest over the cap usually means the conversation should be split into smaller files.

problem: Some checks were skipped because of an earlier problem
what_it_means: Another problem in the same file stopped the later checks from running. This line is here so you know those checks did not happen.
how_it_is_checked: When an earlier check fails in a way that blocks later ones, the app lists which groups of checks did not run.
why_it_matters: Without this note, a short list of findings could be misread as a nearly clean file.
what_to_do: Deal with the other error reported for this file first. The skipped checks will run once it is resolved.
technical_check: Checks skipped because an earlier layer failed
technical_detail: An earlier layer of the file failed, so later checks could not run. The message says which checks were skipped. This is information to read alongside the error that caused it. Fix the error reported for the same file first (damaged MIME, ZIP or manifest); the skipped checks will run once that is resolved.

problem: The one-day and 24-hour checks could not be decided
what_it_means: One or more messages have a missing or unreadable time, so the program could not say whether the file passes the one-day and 24-hour checks. It neither passed nor failed.
how_it_is_checked: Before judging the one-day and 24-hour checks, the app confirms that every message has a readable time.
why_it_matters: With a time missing, either answer could be wrong, so the app reports the checks as undecided instead of guessing.
what_to_do: Ask whoever produced the file to correct the times listed in the finding, then scan again.

what_it_means: The scan was cancelled, or failed, before it reached this file. Nothing is known about it.
how_it_is_checked: When a scan is cancelled or fails, the app records each file it had not yet reached.
why_it_matters: The reports then show exactly which files were never checked.
what_to_do: Run the scan again and let it finish.
